source_text: πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ παρὰ τῷ Χριστῷ μένει, ἀχώριστον ὂν τῇ θείᾳ φύσει· καὶ ὅτι τὰ θεϊκὰ ἔργα ὑπὸ τῆς ἀρρήτου τριάδος ὁμοφρόνως γίνεται· καὶ καθὰ ὁ πατὴρ ἐν ἰδίᾳ ὑποστάσει ὢν ἐξεικονίζεται ἐν τῷ μονογενεῖ, διὰ τὸ ἀπαράλλακτον τῆς θεότητος, τουτέστιν τῆς οὐσίας· τὸν ἴσον τρόπον καὶ ὁ μονογενὴς ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ ἁγίῳ πνεύματι. πόσα δὲ ἄλλα ἐμφέρεται περὶ τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος οὐ διαφέροντα πρὸς τὰ γεγραμμένα περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ μονογενοῦς αὐτοῦ υἱοῦ, ἐξ ὧν τινα διαφόροις τόποις τοῦδε περιέχεται τοῦ βιβλίου, δι' ὧν ἦλθεν ὁ τοῦ λόγου δρόμος. 5.27 ἐπεὶ μή γ' ἔτι ἐροῦσιν ἀντερωτηθέντες, ὅτι ἐκ τοῦ Ἀδὰμ ἡ Εὔα καὶ οἱ ἐξ αὐτῆς παῖδες; καὶ πῶς οἱ μὲν ἐγράφησαν γεννηθέντες, ἡ δὲ οὔτ' αὐτοῦ παῖς, οὔτ' ἀδελφὴ τῶν τεχθέντων ἐκ λήθη; ὁπότε οὐ δυνατὸν παραδειχθῆναι ἐκ παραβολῆς κτισμάτων τὴν μονάδα καὶ ἀσύγκριτον φύσιν, τὴν ἀθέατον μένουσαν τῷ νῷ, ἀκοῇ δὲ καὶ ῥήμασιν οὔτε προοισθῆναι ἀνεχομένην. κἂν γὰρ μικρά τις ὡσεὶ σκιὰ ὁμοιώσεως οἱονείπως. εὑρεθῇ, φεύγει τὸ πλέον ἀφὲν τὸν παρεκβάλλοντα κάτω που. οὐδαμῶς γὰρ τὸ παράδειγμα ταυτότης εἶναι δύναται· ἐκεῖνα δὲ μόνον λέγειν ἀσφαλές, ἅπερ πρὸς τὰ μέτρα ἡμῶν ἐδίδαξαν αἱ γραφαί. 5.28 ὅτι οὖν ἓν καὶ μόνον εἶναι πνεῦμα τοῦ 54 θεοῦ πατρὸς γέγραπται, διὰ τὸ κεχωρίσθαι μὲν τῇ φύσει τῶν ἄλλων πνευμάτων, συνῆφθαι δὲ τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ αὐτοῦ τῷ λόγῳ τῆς οὐσίας, Παῦλος ὑφηγεῖται γράφων πρὸς μὲν Κορινθίους ἐν τῇ πρώτῃ ἐπιστολῇ· «ἄλλῳ δὲ χαρίσματα ἰαμάτων ἐν τῷ ἑνὶ πνεύματι·» καὶ πάλιν· «πάντα δὲ ταῦτα ἐνεργεῖ τὸ ἓν καὶ αὐτὸ πνεῦμα, διαιροῦν ἰδίᾳ ἑκάστῳ, καθὼς βούλεται,» καὶ πάλιν· «πάντες ἓν πνεῦμα ἐποτίσθημεν·» πρὸς δὲ Ἐφεσίους· «ὅτι δι' αὐτοῦ ἔχομεν τὴν προσαγωγὴν οἱ ἀμφότεροι ἐν ἑνὶ πνεύματι πρὸς τὸν πατέρα·» καὶ πάλιν· «σπουδάζοντες τηρεῖν τὴν ἑνότητα τοῦ πνεύματος·» τουτέστιν· πολλὴν ποιεῖσθαι φυλακὴν τοῦ μὴ χωρίζειν αὐτὸ τῆς ἀνωτάτω ἑνάδος καὶ αὐτοτελοῦς οὐσίας. 5.29 ὅτι δὲ καὶ ῥῆμα ὠνόμασται, μαρτυροῦσιν οὑτωσί· Παῦλος γράφων πρὸς Ἐφεσίους μέν· «ἀναλαβόντες τὴν πανοπλίαν τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ θώρακα τῆς δικαιοσύ νης καὶ τὸν θυρεὸν τῆς πίστεως καὶ τὴν περικεφαλαίαν τοῦ σω τηρίου καὶ τὴν μάχαιραν τοῦ πνεύματος, ὅ ἐστιν ῥῆμα θεοῦ.» ἧς τινος μαχαίρας ἐμνημόνευσεν καὶ Ματθαῖος ἐκ προσώπου τοῦ Χριστοῦ εἰπών· «οὐκ ἦλθον βαλεῖν εἰρήνην, ἀλλὰ μάχαιραν·» οὐ ξίφος λέγων, ἀλλὰ τὴν εἰρήνης ἐπέκεινα τμητικὴν τῶν πεπωρωμένων καρδιῶν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος ἀκατάλεκτον σοφίαν· πρὸς δὲ Ἑβραίους· «φέρων γὰρ τὰ πάντα τῷ ῥήματι τῆς δυνάμεως αὐτοῦ.» 5.30 ποίῳ δὲ ῥήματι; προεφήτευσεν ∆αυίδ· «τῷ λόγῳ κυρίου οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἐστερεώθησαν καὶ τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ στόματος αὐτοῦ πᾶσαι αἱ δυνάμεις αὐτῶν·» καὶ πάλιν ὁ Παῦλος· «ἀδύνατον γὰρ τοὺς ἅπαξ φωτισθέντας γευσαμένους τε τῆς δωρεᾶς τῆς ἐπουρανίου καὶ μετόχους γενηθέντας πνεύματος ἁγίου καὶ καλὸν γευσαμένους θεοῦ ῥῆμα·» Πέτρος δέ· «διότι πᾶσα σὰρξ ὡς χόρτος καὶ πᾶσα δόξα αὐτῆς ὡς ἄνθος χόρτου· ἐξηράνθη ὁ χόρτος καὶ τὸ ἄνθος ἐξέπεσεν καὶ ἡ εὐπρέπεια αὐτοῦ ἀπώλετο· τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα τοῦ θεοῦ μένει εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα·» ὃν τρόπον περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ ψάλλει ἐν ριηʹ· «εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα, κύριε, ὁ λόγος σου διαμένει ἐν τῷ οὐρανῷ.» πολλὰ γὰρ περὶ τῶν ἀκροτάτων καὶ θειοτάτων ὑποστάσεων μυστικώτατα παραδίδωσιν. 6.ν Περὶ τοῦ πάντα, ὅσα ἴδια θεότητος, μαρτυρεῖσθαι περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος οὕτως· Ἔπειτα οὖν χρησμῳδοῦσιν περὶ τῆς ἀκηράτου καὶ ἀφράστου φύσεως τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος οἷα περὶ τοῦ ὅλων κατεξουσιάζοντος θεοῦ καὶ πατρὸς καὶ τοῦ πάντων ἐπέκεινα καὶ πάντων κυρίου υἱοῦ, διὰ τὸ μὴ ἑτεροουσίως ἔχειν μηδὲ δυνάμει καὶ δόξῃ ἐλαττόνως. καὶ οὐδὲν εὑρίσκεται τούτων ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ ὑπάρχον οὐδενὶ κτιστῷ. ὅπερ γὰρ καὶ ἔχει, φιλοτιμηθὲν παρὰ τῆς ἐν μιᾷ θεότητι τριάδος ἔχει· καὶ πέφυκεν ἕκαστον ἀεὶ ἀφ' ὧν ἐστιν ἐπιγινώσκεσθαι, τί τέ ἐστιν, καὶ τί μή ἐστιν, εἴτε θεὸς ἔφυ, εἴτε κτίσμα. οἷον· 6.1ν ὅτι οὐ κατὰ αἱρετικοὺς πρῶτον κτίσμα ἐστίν. ἀλλὰ θεός· τὸ γὰρ πρῶτον κτίσμα ὁ σατανᾶς τυγχάνει. ἡ κτίσις τὸ εἶναι ἔχει, οὐκ οὖσα τὴν ἀρχήν. ἐδείχθη δὲ ἐν τῷ Ἰὼβ καὶ ποῖον αὐτῆς ἐστιν ἐν λογικοῖς πρῶτον ποίημα· λέγει γὰρ τὸ ψευσάμενον τῷ τρόπῳ τὴν φύσιν διάβολον. τὸ δ' ἅγιον πνεῦμα ὡς «πνοὴ τοῦ παντοκράτορος» κτίσμα εἶναι ἢ ἀρχὴν ὅλως ἔχειν, οὐδαμῇ γέγραπται. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν προϋπῆρξεν τοῦ δημιουργικοῦ πνεύματος δημιούργημα, καὶ τοιοῦτο
pass_a_gloss: [Continuing from the previous section: 'For observe that, as the Father, so also the'] Spirit of him abides with Christ, being inseparable in the divine nature; and that the divine works come about with one mind by the ineffable Trinity; and as the Father, being in his own hypostasis, is imaged in the Only-begotten, because of the indistinguishableness of the Godhead, that is, of the essence; in the equal manner also the Only-begotten in the one Holy Spirit. And how many other things are brought forward about the divine Spirit not differing from the things written about God and Father and his only-begotten Son, of which some are contained in various places of this book, through which the course of the argument came. 5.27 Since will they not further say, when questioned in turn, that from Adam [came] Eve and the children from her? And how were these written as begotten, but she was called neither his child nor sister of those born? Since it is not possible for the single and incomparable nature to be shown from a comparison of creatures, [the nature] remaining unseen to the mind, and not enduring even to be brought forth to hearing and in words. For even if some small [thing], as it were a shadow of likeness, is found in some way, the greater part escapes, leaving the one who compares somewhere below. For in no way can the example be identity; and it is safe to say only those things which the Scriptures taught toward our measures. 5.28 That therefore the Spirit of [a printed page number 54 stands here in the copy-text] God the Father is written to be one and only, because of being separated by nature from the other spirits, and joined to the Father and to his Son in the account of the essence, Paul instructs, writing to the Corinthians in the first letter: 'and to another gifts of healings in the one Spirit'; and again: 'and all these things the one and same Spirit works, dividing individually to each as it wills'; and again: 'all were given to drink one Spirit'; and to the Ephesians: 'that through him we both have the access in one Spirit to the Father'; and again: 'being eager to keep the unity of the Spirit'; that is, to make much guard of not separating it from the uppermost Unity and self-complete essence. 5.29 And that it has also been named 'utterance', they testify thus: Paul writing to the Ephesians: 'having taken up the full armour of God and breastplate of righteousness and the shield of faith and the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is utterance of God'. Which sword Matthew also mentioned, speaking from the person of Christ: 'I did not come to cast peace, but a sword'; not saying a blade, but the indescribable wisdom of the Holy Spirit, beyond peace, cutting of hardened hearts; and to the Hebrews: 'for bearing all things by the utterance of his power'. 5.30 And by what utterance? David prophesied: 'by the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers'; and again Paul: 'for it is impossible [for] those once enlightened and having tasted the heavenly gift and having become partakers of Holy Spirit and having tasted the good utterance of God'; and Peter: 'because all flesh [is] as grass and all its glory as flower of grass; the grass withered and the flower fell off and its comeliness perished; but the utterance of God abides for ever'; in which manner he sings about the Son in the 118th [Psalm, Greek numbering]: 'for ever, Lord, your word abides in heaven'. For it hands down many things about the highest and most divine hypostases most mystically. 6.ν [Chapter title:] About everything that is proper to Godhead being attested about the Holy Spirit thus: Next then they declare about the pure and inexpressible nature of the Holy Spirit such things as about the God and Father who holds authority over all things and the Son beyond all and Lord of all, because of its not being of another essence nor lesser in power and glory. And none of these is found belonging of itself to any created thing. For what it does have, it has bestowed in honour by the Trinity in one Godhead; and each is by nature always to be recognized from the things it is, both what it is and what it is not, whether it is by nature God or creature. For example: 6.1ν [Chapter title:] That it is not, according to heretics, first creature, but God. For the first creature happens to be Satan. The creation has being, not being at the beginning. And it was shown in Job also which is its first thing made among rational beings; for it speaks of the devil who belied his nature by his conduct. But that the Holy Spirit, as 'breath of the Almighty', is a creature or has a beginning at all is nowhere written. For a thing made would not have existed before the making Spirit, and such a [continues in the next section: 'worthless, ungrateful and profane' notion] ...
pass_b_english: …his Spirit abides with Christ, being inseparable in the divine nature; and that the divine works are done by the ineffable Trinity with one mind; and that, as the Father, existing in his own hypostasis, is imaged in the Only-begotten because their Godhead, that is, their essence, is without difference, in the same way the Only-begotten is imaged in the one Holy Spirit. And how many other things are set down about the divine Spirit that do not differ from what is written about God the Father and his only-begotten Son! Some of them are contained in various places of this book, through which the course of the argument has passed.

Besides, when they are questioned in turn, will they not say that Eve, and the children born of her, came from Adam? How then were the children written as begotten, while she was called neither his child nor the sister of those who were born? Yet the single and incomparable nature cannot be shown by a comparison drawn from creatures, since it remains unseen by the mind and does not allow itself even to be brought forth to the hearing or in words. For even if some small shadow of a likeness, so to speak, is found in some way, the greater part escapes and leaves the one who draws the comparison somewhere far below. An example can never be identity. It is safe to say only those things which the Scriptures have taught, to the measure of our capacity.

That the Spirit of God the Father is written to be one and only, because he is separated by nature from the other spirits and joined to the Father and his Son in the very account of essence, Paul teaches. He writes to the Corinthians in the first letter: “to another gifts of healing in the one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:9); and again: “All these things the one and the same Spirit works, dividing to each one individually as he wills” (1 Corinthians 12:11); and again: “We were all made to drink of one Spirit” (1 Corinthians 12:13). To the Ephesians he writes: “for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father” (Ephesians 2:18); and again: “eager to keep the unity of the Spirit” (Ephesians 4:3), that is, to take great care not to separate him from the supreme Unity and self-complete essence.

That he is also named “utterance,” they bear witness in this way. Paul writes to the Ephesians: “Taking up the whole armour of God, and the breastplate of righteousness, and the shield of faith, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the utterance of God” (Ephesians 6:13–17). Matthew too mentioned this sword, speaking in the person of Christ: “I did not come to bring peace, but a sword” (Matthew 10:34). He does not mean a blade, but the indescribable wisdom of the Holy Spirit, which reaches beyond peace and cuts through hardened hearts. And Paul writes to the Hebrews: “upholding all things by the utterance of his power” (Hebrews 1:3).

By what utterance? David prophesied: “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their powers” (Psalm 33:6). And again Paul: “For it is impossible for those who were once enlightened, who have tasted the heavenly gift and become partakers of the Holy Spirit, and have tasted the good utterance of God” (Hebrews 6:4–5). And Peter: “For all flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass withered and the flower fell, and its beauty perished; but the utterance of God abides for ever” (1 Peter 1:24–25). In the same way the Psalmist sings of the Son in the hundred and nineteenth Psalm: “For ever, O Lord, your word abides in heaven” (Psalm 119:89). For Scripture hands down many things, in a most hidden way, about the highest and most divine hypostases.
That everything proper to the Godhead is attested of the Holy Spirit, as follows.

Next, then, the Scriptures declare about the pure and inexpressible nature of the Holy Spirit such things as they declare about God the Father, who holds sway over all, and about the Son, who is beyond all and Lord of all, because he is not of another essence, nor less in power and glory. And none of these things is found to belong of itself to any created thing. For whatever a creature does have, it has as a gift bestowed by the Trinity in one Godhead. And each thing can always be recognized from what belongs to it: what it is and what it is not, whether it is God by nature or a creature. For example:
That he is not the first creature, as the heretics say, but God.

For the first creature is Satan. Creation has being, though at first it was not; and it was shown in Job which is the first thing made among rational beings, for the book speaks of the devil, who belied his nature by his conduct. But that the Holy Spirit, as “breath of the Almighty” (Job 33:4), is a creature or has any beginning at all is nowhere written. lemmas.gloss: be imaged, be represented as in an image
utterance, spoken word (kept distinct from λόγος, Word)
bestow as an honour, give freely
thing made, product of a maker

choices.issue: Garbled draft, chapter titles run into the text, edition numbers printed, broken sentence, abbreviated references
choices.choice: 2026-11-11 (claude-sumfix2-e-u13): retranslated from the Greek. The old English printed 5.27, 5.28 and 5.29 inside the reading text, broke 5.29 off at 'the ma-' and restarted with 'rejoicing in the Spirit', and ran the chapter titles 6.ν and 6.1ν into the text. Mistranslations fixed: ἐκ λήθη (ἐκλήθη, 'was called') as 'born from oblivion'; 'one must flee from the more abundant, leaving the one who drives downward' (the greater part escapes, leaving the one who compares below); 'Paul is directed'; 'that it does not divide itself' (not to separate him); 'the peace of the sanctified hearts' (cuts through hardened hearts); 'what kind of thing it is in logical terms: first, a poem' (the first thing made among rational beings); 'exist of itself from nothing to any creature'. References: (1 Cor 12:11), (1 Cor 12:13), (Eph 2:18), (Eph 4:3), (Matt 10:34), (Heb 1:3), (Ps 33:6) written out; (Heb 6:4-5) -> Hebrews 6:4–5; (1 Pet 1:24) -> 1 Peter 1:24–25 (the quotation ends with 1:25); 'in the Psalms' -> 'the hundred and nineteenth Psalm' (Greek 118); Ephesians 6:13–17 and Job 33:4 added.

choices.term: πνεῦμα αὐτοῦ παρὰ τῷ Χριστῷ μένει
choices.english: …his Spirit abides with Christ
choices.why: The sentence begins in the previous section ('For observe that, as the Father, so too the …'): as the Father abides in Christ (John 14:10, just quoted), so does his Spirit. Only the words this section holds are translated, opened with '…'.

choices.term: ἐπεὶ μή γ' ἔτι ἐροῦσιν ἀντερωτηθέντες
choices.english: Besides, when they are questioned in turn, will they not say
choices.why: Didymus turns to the objection of 5.1 (if the Spirit were from the Father's hypostasis, he would be the Son's brother): Eve came from Adam without being begotten or called a sister of Adam's sons.

choices.english: was called
choices.why: A word split by the copy-text (ἐκλήθη); the old 'from oblivion' read it as two words.

choices.english: in some way, is found
choices.why: The stray full stop inside the clause is copy-text debris.

choices.english: some small shadow of a likeness, so to speak
choices.why: ὡσεί, 'as it were', is Didymus' hedge; kept as 'so to speak'.

choices.english: the Spirit of God
choices.why: 54 is a printed page number in the copy-text, skipped.

choices.english: in the very account of essence
choices.why: 'By the definition of essence': the Spirit is joined to Father and Son in what essence is, not by grace. The phrase could also be read 'his Son the Word, in essence'; the dative after a comma-less series favours 'in the account of essence'.

choices.english: utterance
choices.why: Didymus' point is the title ῥῆμα for the Spirit, distinct from λόγος for the Son; 'utterance' is kept in every quotation where ῥῆμα stands (Ephesians 6:17, Hebrews 1:3, Hebrews 6:5, 1 Peter 1:25), and 'word' where λόγος stands (Psalm 33:6, Psalm 119:89).

choices.english: they bear witness
choices.why: Plural: the apostles (Paul and Matthew) whose texts follow.

choices.term: τὴν εἰρήνης ἐπέκεινα τμητικὴν τῶν πεπωρωμένων καρδιῶν ... σοφίαν
choices.english: the indescribable wisdom of the Holy Spirit, which reaches beyond peace and cuts through hardened hearts
choices.why: τμητικήν governs the hardened hearts; εἰρήνης ἐπέκεινα, 'beyond peace', answers Matthew's 'not peace but a sword'.

choices.english: the Spirit of his mouth (Psalm 33:6)
choices.why: Didymus reads πνεῦμα in Psalm 32:6 (Greek numbering; 33:6 English) as the Holy Spirit, here identified with God's 'utterance'; 'Spirit' rather than 'breath' carries his argument.

choices.english: in the hundred and nineteenth Psalm
choices.why: Greek Psalm 118 is Psalm 119 in English numbering; the number is converted, as in u03-rem-mid.

choices.english: For Scripture hands down many things
choices.why: The verb has no expressed subject; Scripture (or the Psalmist) is meant.

choices.term: 6.ν Περὶ τοῦ πάντα, ὅσα ἴδια θεότητος, μαρτυρεῖσθαι ...
choices.english: That everything proper to the Godhead is attested of the Holy Spirit, as follows.
choices.why: Chapter title, set as its own paragraph.

choices.english: the Scriptures declare
choices.why: Plural verb without a subject; the inspired writers are meant, as in the previous paragraphs.

choices.english: For whatever a creature does have
choices.why: The subject is the created thing of the previous clause; English names it.

choices.term: 6.1ν ὅτι οὐ κατὰ αἱρετικοὺς πρῶτον κτίσμα ἐστίν. ἀλλὰ θεός·
choices.english: That he is not the first creature, as the heretics say, but God.
choices.why: Chapter title, set as its own paragraph; 'but God' is read as the end of the title (the copy-text's full stop before ἀλλά is debris), and the body begins 'For the first creature is Satan.'

choices.english: though at first it was not
choices.why: τὴν ἀρχήν adverbial, 'at the beginning'; creation came to be from not being.

choices.term: τὸ ψευσάμενον τῷ τρόπῳ τὴν φύσιν διάβολον
choices.english: the devil, who belied his nature by his conduct
choices.why: He falsified by his way of life the good nature he was made with.

choices.english: and such a …
choices.why: The sentence runs into the next section ('worthless, ungrateful and profane' notion); only the words this section holds are translated, ending with '…'.
